initial_observation.encounter_context: presented to the emergency room of our hospital
initial_observation.chief_complaint: brief episodes of sudden speechlessness and hoarseness
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: Since 3 months, he noticed a progressively hoarse voice when talking to his passengers or became even speechless for several seconds, experiencing dyspnoea during these episodes. Additionally, he reported vomiting particularly after swallowing cold water and progressive spasms of his hands with cramps during driving. At presentation, the hoarseness and sudden disappearance of speech were present up to eight times a day lasting 30–40 seconds. No paresthesias or seizures were experienced. Physical and neurological examination showed no abnormalities except for a positive Chvostek’s and Trousseau’s sign.

evidence_items.source_text: Since 3 months, he noticed a progressively hoarse voice when talking to his passengers or became even speechless for several seconds. During these episodes, he also experienced dyspnoea. Additionally, he reported problem of vomiting, particularly after swallowing cold water. Further questioning revealed progressive spasms of his hands, often during driving, of such severity that his hands were cramped around his steering wheel without the ability to loosen them.
General physical and neurological examination showed no abnormalities except for a positive Chvostek’s and Trousseau’s sign (see figure 1).

Blood tests at presentation showed a severe low total calcium (1.03 mmol/L; reference range 2.2–2.6), normal albumin (40 g/L; reference range 35–55), raised phosphate (2.21 mmol/L; reference range 0.70–1.40), raised CK (2962 IU/L; reference range <170) and low magnesium (0.58 mmol/L; reference range 0.7–1.0) with normal kidney and liver function tests.

Later blood tests showed hypoparathyroidism (0.7 pmol/L; reference range 2–7) and low 25-hydroxy(OH)-vitamin D3 concentrations (11 nmol; reference range 50–100). ECG showed a prolonged QTc interval of 501 ms.
Further investigations of his hypoparathyroidism showed no mutations of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) and no parathyroid antibodies.

Immediate treatment with calcium gluconate and magnesium sulphate intravenously was given in the emergency department while monitoring the patient’s heart. Quickly after administration of calcium, his voice improved.
We admitted the patient to the acute care unit where he continued to receive calcium intravenously together with alphacalcidol (1 μg) since his blood test showed hypoparathyroidism and cholecalciferol orally to restore his vitamin D concentration. After 24 hours, he received 20 mmol calcium in total, which resulted in plasma calcium of 1.57 mmol/L (reference range: 2.20–2.65 mmol/L) and a normal QTc interval. He was transferred to the hospital ward where he continued to receive calcium (10 mmol/24 hours) intravenously and alphacalcidol (1 ug) orally. After 5 days, his plasma calcium normalised (2.15 mmol/L) together with normalisation of his creatine kinase level, and he was discharged.

Our patient was diagnosed with idiopathic primary hypoparathyroidism for which life-long treatment with calcium supplements and alphacalcidol was prescribed. Since there was a vitamin D deficiency present, he received vitamin D supplements as well. At 2 weeks after discharge, the patient was able to return to his work as a taxi driver.
Follow-up was needed at 1 week, 1 month and every 2 months thereafter in the first year after discharge, on which his calcium, vitamin D levels and urine were checked. Calcium levels above 2.10 mmol/L were aimed for. However, during follow-up, our patient experienced adherence problems, resulting in hypocalcaemia and again rhabdomyolysis, both normalising after intensification of his treatment. Further follow-up 2 years after hospitalisation showed better adherence with normal plasma calcium and CK concentrations. As well, no vitamin D deficiency or toxicity, or hypercalciuria were seen during follow-up.

diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: These blood tests, together with no medical or surgical history, made a diagnosis of primary hypoparathyroidism with a concomitant vitamin D deficiency most likely. We considered autoimmune hypoparathyroidism or a mutation in the CaSR as a cause of his hypoparathyroidism. However, both tests were negative, resulting in the final diagnosis of idiopathic primary hypoparathyroidism.
